questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: Which is the highest (largest) category in the taxonomic hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Kingdom is the broadest category and includes several phyla.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: A group of related genera is placed in a
questions.explanation: Related genera form a family, and related families form an order.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: Growth in living organisms differs from that in non-living objects because living things grow
options: from inside, by cell division or cell enlargement
by sticking material on the outside
only in size, never in number of cells
only in the presence of light
questions.explanation: Non-living objects such as a mountain or a sand mound grow by accumulation of material on the surface.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: The sum total of all the chemical reactions occurring in the body of a living organism is called
questions.explanation: Metabolism is a defining feature of all living organisms.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: Why is reproduction NOT accepted as a defining feature that applies to every living organism?
options: Some living organisms, such as mules and worker bees, do not reproduce
questions.explanation: Mules and worker bees are alive but sterile, so reproduction cannot define all living things.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: A student isolates metabolic enzymes from cells and carries out the reactions in a test tube. These reactions are
options: living reactions, but the test tube contents are not a living organism
non-living reactions that do not need enzymes
proof that the test tube is alive
questions.explanation: Isolated metabolic reactions in vitro are living reactions, but not a living organism.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: How does the growth of a living organism differ from the growth of a non-living object? Give an example of each.
questions.answer: Living organisms grow from inside by cell division and enlargement, e.g. a seedling; non-living objects grow only by accumulation of material on the outside, e.g. a mountain or a sand pile.
questions.explanation: Growth in living things is intrinsic.

questions.topic: The Living World and Biological Classification
questions.q: Why do classification systems of organisms keep changing as new information is gathered?
questions.answer: Classification is based on characters such as cell structure, body organisation, reproduction and evolutionary relationships. As new characters are found through better tools and studies, groups are re-arranged to show natural relationships better.
keyPoints: Groups are revised to show relationships
questions.explanation: Whittaker's five kingdoms replaced the earlier two-kingdom system for this reason.

questions.q: Which group of algae has chlorophyll a and b and stores starch, like higher plants?
questions.explanation: Green algae (Chlorophyceae) have chlorophyll a and b and store starch.

questions.q: Floridean starch is the stored food of
questions.explanation: Red algae (Rhodophyceae) store floridean starch.

questions.q: Peat, used as fuel and as packing material for living plants, is obtained from
questions.explanation: Sphagnum, a moss, accumulates as peat and holds much water.

questions.q: A typical mature embryo sac of an angiosperm contains how many cells?
questions.explanation: The embryo sac is seven-celled and eight-nucleate.

questions.q: Gymnosperms do not depend on water for fertilisation, because
options: their male gametes are flagellated and swim in air
the pollen tube carries non-motile male gametes to the egg
they are fertilised by the sporophyte
questions.explanation: Pollen tubes deliver the male gametes directly to the egg in seed plants.

questions.q: A plant has a dominant, multicellular diploid sporophyte, while its gametophyte is reduced to a few cells. Its life cycle is
questions.explanation: In a diplontic cycle the diploid phase dominates, as in gymnosperms and angiosperms.

questions.q: Mention three ways in which algae are useful to humans.
questions.answer: Algae carry out about half of the photosynthesis on earth and add oxygen; some, like Porphyra and Laminaria, are food; agar and algin come from red and brown algae; Chlorella is a protein supplement.
keyPoints: Source of agar, algin or single-cell protein
questions.explanation: Algae are also primary producers in water.

questions.q: How does the seed habit help plants to survive better than spore-producing plants?
questions.answer: A seed protects the embryo with a seed coat, contains stored food for the young plant, and has a dormant state that helps it survive unfavourable conditions and be dispersed; it also frees fertilisation from the need for water.
questions.explanation: The seed habit is a major evolutionary advance.

questions.q: The numerous small pores on the body wall of a sponge are called
questions.explanation: Water enters through ostia and leaves through the osculum.

questions.q: Fishes breathe through
questions.explanation: Fishes have gills for respiration in water.

questions.q: Which flatworm has hooks and suckers for attaching to the host's intestine?
questions.explanation: The tapeworm Taenia has a scolex with hooks and suckers.

questions.q: The roundworms, which have a pseudocoelom, belong to phylum
questions.explanation: Aschelminthes (roundworms), e.g. Ascaris, are pseudocoelomates with separate sexes.

questions.q: A bat flies but is classified as a mammal rather than a bird because it
options: has mammary glands, hair and gives birth to young
questions.explanation: Mammary glands, hair and viviparity are mammalian features; flight is not a deciding character.

questions.q: Marine animals with eight rows of ciliated comb plates for locomotion and the ability to show bioluminescence belong to
questions.explanation: Ctenophores, or comb jellies, move with comb plates.

questions.q: List any three characteristics of phylum Arthropoda.
questions.answer: Arthropods have a chitinous exoskeleton, jointed appendages and a segmented body with an open circulatory system; they are bilaterally symmetrical and have a haemocoel.
questions.explanation: Arthropoda is the largest phylum.

questions.q: Birds and mammals are called homeotherms. What does this mean and how does it help them?
questions.answer: They keep a constant body temperature irrespective of the surroundings; this lets them stay active and live in a wide range of habitats, hot or cold.
keyPoints: Allows a wide range of habitats
questions.explanation: Other vertebrates are poikilotherms.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: The embryonic part of a seed that grows into the root is the
questions.explanation: The radicle forms the primary root, and the plumule forms the shoot.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: The potato is a modified
questions.explanation: The potato tuber is a swollen underground stem with buds (eyes).

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: The corolla of a pea flower is described as
questions.explanation: Pea has five petals: a standard, two wings and two keel petals, forming a papilionaceous corolla.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: The only living component of xylem is
questions.explanation: Tracheids, vessels and fibres are dead at maturity; xylem parenchyma is living.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: In the periderm of a woody stem, the phelloderm (secondary cortex) is formed
options: on the inner side of the cork cambium
questions.explanation: Phellogen cuts off phellem outwards and phelloderm inwards.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: In a dicot root, the xylem is described as exarch, which means that
options: xylem and phloem are in the same bundle
protoxylem lies towards the periphery and metaxylem towards the centre
questions.explanation: In roots, protoxylem is outer and metaxylem is inner (exarch condition).

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: Differentiate between a simple leaf and a compound leaf with one example of each.
questions.answer: In a simple leaf the lamina is entire or incised but not cut to the midrib, as in mango; in a compound leaf the incisions reach the midrib or petiole, breaking the lamina into leaflets, as in neem.
questions.explanation: A bud is present in the axil of a leaf but not of a leaflet.

questions.topic: Morphology and Anatomy of Flowering Plants
questions.q: What are bulliform cells? How do they help a grass leaf survive water shortage?
questions.answer: Bulliform cells are large, empty, colourless cells in the upper epidermis of grass leaves. When they lose water the leaf curls inward, reducing the surface exposed and so lowering water loss.
keyPoints: Large colourless cells in the upper epidermis
Flaccid cells make the leaf roll
questions.explanation: They are a feature of the isobilateral monocot leaf.

questions.q: The mature bone cells are called
questions.explanation: Osteocytes lie in lacunae in the hard bone matrix.

questions.q: Cartilage cells are called
questions.explanation: Chondrocytes lie in small cavities in the solid but pliable cartilage matrix.

questions.q: How many pairs of walking legs does a cockroach have?
questions.explanation: Each thoracic segment bears a pair of legs, so a cockroach has three pairs.

questions.q: The mouth parts of a cockroach are of the
questions.explanation: Cockroach mouthparts include labrum, mandibles, maxillae and labium for chewing.

questions.q: The epithelium that lines the ducts of glands and the tubular parts of nephrons, and helps in secretion and absorption, is
questions.explanation: Cuboidal epithelium has cube-shaped cells and is found in ducts of glands and nephron tubules.

questions.q: The fertilised eggs of a cockroach are enclosed in a capsule called the
questions.explanation: A female cockroach produces ootheca, each containing about 14 to 16 eggs.

questions.q: Distinguish between a tendon and a ligament.
questions.answer: A tendon is dense regular connective tissue connecting skeletal muscle to bone; a ligament is dense regular connective tissue connecting one bone to another bone.
keyPoints: Both are dense regular connective tissue
questions.explanation: Both are made of collagen fibres arranged in parallel rows.

questions.q: How do intercalated discs help the heart to work as a unit?
questions.answer: Intercalated discs join neighbouring cardiac muscle cells and contain gap junctions that let the impulse pass quickly from cell to cell, so that all the cells contract almost together.
keyPoints: Gap junctions allow quick spread of impulse
questions.explanation: This ensures coordinated beating.

questions.q: The cell organelle where proteins are synthesised is the
questions.explanation: Ribosomes translate mRNA into proteins.

questions.q: The membrane that bounds the vacuole in a plant cell is called the
questions.explanation: The tonoplast is the single membrane around the vacuole.

questions.q: Each centriole has a cartwheel-like structure made of
options: nine doublet microtubules around two central ones
nine evenly spaced triplets of microtubules
questions.explanation: A centriole has nine peripheral triplet fibrils and no central tubules (9+0).

questions.q: The axoneme of cilia and flagella shows the arrangement
questions.explanation: Nine peripheral doublets surround two central singlet microtubules.

questions.q: Cells of the adrenal cortex, which make steroid hormones, would be expected to have abundant
questions.explanation: SER is the site of lipid and steroid synthesis.

questions.q: In a chloroplast, the chlorophyll pigments are located in the
questions.explanation: Thylakoids of the grana carry the photosynthetic pigments.

questions.q: Describe the structure of a chloroplast.
questions.answer: A chloroplast has a double membrane envelope enclosing the stroma, which contains DNA, ribosomes and enzymes; inside are flattened thylakoids stacked into grana and joined by stroma lamellae. Chlorophyll is in the thylakoid membranes.
questions.explanation: The chloroplast is the site of photosynthesis.

questions.q: Why do lipid-soluble substances cross the plasma membrane more easily than ions?
questions.answer: The plasma membrane has a lipid bilayer, so non-polar, lipid-soluble substances dissolve in it and pass through; polar molecules and ions are repelled by the hydrophobic core and need carrier or channel proteins.
questions.explanation: This makes the membrane selectively permeable.

questions.q: Fats are esters of fatty acids with
questions.explanation: A triglyceride is made of glycerol joined to three fatty acids.

questions.q: The pentose sugar present in RNA is
questions.explanation: RNA contains ribose; DNA contains 2-deoxyribose.

questions.q: Starch forms a blue colour when treated with
questions.explanation: Iodine is held in the helical starch molecule, producing a blue-black colour.

questions.q: Nucleotides in a nucleic acid strand are linked together by
questions.explanation: The phosphate group links the 3' carbon of one sugar and the 5' carbon of the next.

questions.q: Enzymes are usually stored at low temperature rather than at high temperature, because low temperature
options: temporarily reduces activity but preserves the structure
questions.explanation: High temperature denatures enzymes; low temperature only slows them, and the effect is reversible.

questions.q: The number of peptide bonds in a polypeptide chain of 150 amino acids is
questions.explanation: A linear chain of n amino acids has n minus 1 peptide bonds.

questions.q: Describe the structure of a nucleotide and how a polynucleotide chain is formed.
questions.answer: A nucleotide is a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group. Nucleotides join through phosphodiester bonds between the phosphate of one and the sugar of the next, forming a polynucleotide.
questions.explanation: DNA and RNA are polynucleotides.

questions.q: Using the idea of the transition state, explain how an enzyme speeds up a reaction.
questions.answer: The substrate must reach a high-energy transition state before turning into product, which needs activation energy. The enzyme binds the substrate at its active site and stabilises the transition state, lowering the energy barrier so the reaction is faster, but the energy difference between substrate and product is unchanged.
questions.explanation: Enzymes do not change the equilibrium.

questions.q: The phase of the cell cycle that follows mitosis and precedes DNA replication is
questions.explanation: The interphase order is G1, S, G2.

questions.q: In animal cells, the spindle apparatus is organised by the
questions.explanation: The centrosome with its centrioles organises the microtubules of the spindle.

questions.q: The X-shaped structures called chiasmata become visible in the stage of
questions.explanation: In diplotene the homologues separate partially but stay held at chiasmata.

questions.q: If the amount of DNA in a G1 cell is 2C, the amount in the same cell at G2 is
questions.explanation: DNA doubles in the S phase, and the chromosome number stays the same.

questions.q: A diploid cell has 2C DNA in G1. The DNA content of each cell at the end of meiosis I is
questions.explanation: After replication the cell has 4C; meiosis I halves it to 2C per cell, and meiosis II to C.

questions.q: The stage of meiotic prophase I that ends with the breakdown of the nuclear envelope and the nucleolus, and has terminalisation of chiasmata, is
questions.explanation: Diakinesis is the last stage of prophase I, just before metaphase I.

questions.q: State the significance of mitosis.
questions.answer: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number constant in daughter cells; it allows growth of the organism, replacement of old or damaged cells and, in plants, continuous growth by meristems.
questions.explanation: Mitosis produces genetically identical cells.

questions.q: Give three differences between mitosis and meiosis.
questions.answer: Mitosis occurs in somatic cells and has one division giving two identical diploid cells with no crossing over; meiosis occurs in germ cells, has two divisions, gives four haploid cells and includes crossing over.
keyPoints: Two diploid or four haploid cells
questions.explanation: Meiosis creates variation and halves chromosome number.

questions.q: Which of the following is a C4 plant?
questions.explanation: Maize, sugarcane and sorghum are C4 plants.

questions.q: The metal present in the chlorophyll molecule is
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll has a porphyrin head with a magnesium atom at the centre.

questions.q: The water-splitting complex of photosystem II requires which of these ions?
questions.explanation: Manganese is needed for the oxygen-evolving complex, along with Cl- and Ca2+.

questions.q: The regeneration of RuBP, the CO2 acceptor, in the Calvin cycle requires
questions.explanation: Regeneration needs one ATP for phosphorylation of ribulose-5-phosphate.

questions.q: Which plants show a higher rate of photosynthesis at high temperature and high light intensity?
questions.explanation: C4 plants have a higher temperature optimum and no photorespiration loss.

questions.q: The number of ATP molecules required in the Calvin cycle for making one molecule of glucose is
questions.explanation: Each CO2 needs 3 ATP, so 6 CO2 need 18 ATP (and 12 NADPH).

questions.q: Name the three stages of the Calvin cycle and state what happens in each.
questions.answer: Carboxylation: CO2 combines with RuBP to form 3-PGA, catalysed by RuBisCO. Reduction: ATP and NADPH reduce 3-PGA to triose phosphate. Regeneration: RuBP is formed again, using ATP.
questions.explanation: The cycle is also called the C3 pathway.

questions.q: Explain Kranz anatomy and its role in C4 photosynthesis.
questions.answer: In C4 leaves, large bundle sheath cells form a ring around the vascular bundles with mesophyll cells outside. CO2 is first fixed in mesophyll as a four-carbon acid, which moves to the bundle sheath where it releases CO2 for the Calvin cycle, concentrating CO2 near RuBisCO.
keyPoints: Bundle sheath cells around the vascular bundles
CO2 released in bundle sheath for the Calvin cycle
questions.explanation: This reduces photorespiration.

questions.q: The number of pyruvic acid molecules produced from one glucose molecule in glycolysis is
questions.explanation: The six-carbon glucose splits into two three-carbon pyruvates.

questions.q: During strenuous exercise, when oxygen is short, muscle cells convert pyruvic acid into
questions.explanation: Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactic acid.

questions.q: According to the NCERT account, the oxidation of one NADH molecule in the electron transport chain gives rise to
questions.explanation: NADH gives about 3 ATP and FADH2 gives 2 ATP in the simple textbook account.

questions.q: Pyruvic acid is converted into acetyl CoA in the
questions.explanation: Oxidative decarboxylation by pyruvate dehydrogenase takes place in the matrix.

questions.q: Fatty acids from the breakdown of fats enter the respiratory pathway as
questions.explanation: Fatty acids are broken down to acetyl CoA, and glycerol enters as PGAL.

questions.q: A poison blocks the transfer of electrons to oxygen by cytochrome c oxidase. The immediate effect is that
options: glycolysis stops completely in the nucleus
the electron transport chain stops and mitochondrial ATP synthesis falls
questions.explanation: Without the final acceptor, electrons back up and the proton gradient cannot be maintained.

questions.q: Write the overall equation for aerobic respiration of glucose.
questions.answer: C6H12O6 + 6 O2 gives 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy (about 38 ATP in the textbook account).
questions.explanation: This is the complete oxidation of glucose.

questions.q: Why is glycolysis described as the common pathway of aerobic and anaerobic respiration?
questions.answer: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and does not need oxygen. It is the first step in both, converting glucose to pyruvic acid; later steps differ, as pyruvate goes to the Krebs cycle with oxygen or to fermentation without it.
keyPoints: Occurs in the cytoplasm without oxygen
questions.explanation: Glycolysis is present in all living cells.

questions.q: Gibberellins were first discovered from the fungus
questions.explanation: Rice seedlings infected by Gibberella grew abnormally tall, leading to the discovery of gibberellins.

questions.q: Zeatin, isolated from maize kernels, is a type of
questions.explanation: Zeatin is a natural cytokinin.

questions.q: Which hormones promote the shedding (abscission) of leaves and fruits?
questions.explanation: Abscisic acid and ethylene promote abscission.

questions.q: Stem cuttings are dipped in a rooting powder containing
questions.explanation: Auxins promote the formation of adventitious roots.

questions.q: The synthetic auxin 2,4-D is used to kill
options: dicot weeds in a monocot crop field
questions.explanation: 2,4-D is a selective herbicide that kills broad-leaved dicot weeds in cereal fields.

questions.q: A root grows by arithmetic growth at 2 cm per day. If its initial length is 5 cm, its length after 4 days will be
questions.explanation: Length = 5 + (2 x 4) = 13 cm, from Lt = L0 + rt.

questions.q: List three physiological effects of auxins.
questions.answer: Auxins promote cell elongation and apical dominance, cause rooting in cuttings, induce parthenocarpy and flowering in pineapple, and prevent premature fruit drop.
keyPoints: Parthenocarpy or prevention of fruit drop
questions.explanation: IAA and IBA are natural auxins.

questions.q: Why is water considered the most important external factor for plant growth?
questions.answer: Water gives the turgidity needed for cell enlargement, is the medium for enzyme action and nutrient transport, and is a raw material in metabolism; growth stops when water is scarce.
questions.explanation: Water, oxygen and nutrients are the main requirements.

questions.q: Which pancreatic enzyme digests proteins in the small intestine?
questions.explanation: Trypsin, from the inactive trypsinogen, digests proteins into peptides.

questions.q: The oxygen-carrying pigment in human blood is found in
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin is present inside erythrocytes.

questions.q: Fats absorbed in the intestinal villi enter the
questions.explanation: Fatty acids and glycerol are made into chylomicrons and enter the lymphatic lacteals.

questions.q: Oxygenated blood from the lungs returns to the heart and enters the
questions.explanation: Pulmonary veins open into the left atrium.

questions.q: A blood pressure reading of 140/90 mm Hg or more in a person at rest indicates
questions.explanation: Normal blood pressure is 120/80, and 140/90 or higher is hypertension.

questions.q: During inspiration, the pressure inside the lungs becomes
options: equal to the pressure in the blood
questions.explanation: Thoracic volume increases, lung pressure falls below atmospheric pressure and air rushes in.

questions.q: What is emulsification of fats? Which secretion brings it about?
questions.answer: Emulsification is the breaking of large fat globules into very small droplets so that lipase can act on a large surface area. Bile salts from the liver do this.
questions.explanation: Bile contains no digestive enzymes.

questions.q: CO2 is about 20 to 25 times more soluble than O2 in water. How does this affect its diffusion across the alveolar membrane?
questions.answer: Because CO2 dissolves much more easily in the membrane and fluids, a small difference in partial pressure is enough for it to diffuse as fast as oxygen does across the diffusion membrane.
questions.explanation: Solubility affects the diffusion rate.

questions.q: The part of the brain that regulates body temperature, hunger and thirst is the
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus contains centres for temperature, hunger and thirst.

questions.q: The hormone secreted by the alpha cells of the pancreas that raises blood glucose is
questions.explanation: Glucagon stimulates glycogenolysis and raises blood sugar.

questions.q: Most of the reabsorption of the glomerular filtrate takes place in the
questions.explanation: The PCT reabsorbs nearly all glucose and amino acids and about 70 to 80 per cent of the electrolytes and water.

questions.q: The part of the hindbrain that coordinates balance and posture is the
questions.explanation: The cerebellum controls balance, posture and fine movements.

questions.q: The descending limb of the loop of Henle is
options: permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes
permeable to electrolytes but not to water
questions.explanation: Water leaves the descending limb and the filtrate becomes concentrated.

questions.q: Deficiency of thyroid hormone in infancy results in stunted growth and mental retardation, a condition called
questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism during development causes cretinism.

questions.q: Name the three major parts of the human brain and give one function of each.
questions.answer: Forebrain (cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus) for thinking and sensation; midbrain for visual and auditory reflexes; hindbrain (pons, cerebellum, medulla) for balance and for control of breathing and heartbeat.
keyPoints: Hindbrain, with a function for each
questions.explanation: The medulla oblongata controls respiration and cardiovascular reflexes.

questions.q: Explain briefly how the loop of Henle and vasa recta help to produce concentrated urine.
questions.answer: The two limbs of the loop of Henle and the vasa recta run in opposite directions, forming a counter-current that builds a rising osmotic gradient of NaCl and urea in the medullary interstitium; water leaves the collecting duct into this gradient, concentrating the urine.
keyPoints: Counter-current flow in the loop and vasa recta
Water reabsorbed from the collecting duct
questions.explanation: Humans can produce urine about four times more concentrated than the filtrate.
